This notebook includes the code for the Bayesian Workflow book
Chapter 17 *Prior specification for regression models: Reanalysis
of sleep study*.

## Introduction

Prior distributions are at the heart of Bayesian statistics and are
mentioned as one of its defining features in almost all
introductions. Yet, in practice, specifying priors remains a highly
challenging and complex topic that tends to cause a lot of
confusion for people having to deal with it. In this case study, we
clarify some of this confusion by explaining the different purposes
of priors and things that should be considered when specifying
them.

**Load packages**

## The sleep study data

We analyze the `sleepstudy` data set
[@Belenky-Wesensten-Thorne-etal:2003] that is shipped with the R
package `lme4` [@Bates-Maechler-Bolker-etal:2015]. The dataset
covers 18 people undergoing sleep deprivation (less than 3 hours of
sleep per night) for 7 consecutive nights, with their average
reaction times in milliseconds in a simple experiment.

Reasons for choosing the `sleepstudy` data set:

- Few variables all of which are easy to understand
- easy yet important multilevel structure 
- sensible to express with both linear and generalized linear models
- non-trivial error distributions
- independent priors are sensible(ish) due to the small number of parameters
- well known to a lot of R users

Days 0-1 were adaptation and training (T1/T2), day 2 was baseline (B);
sleep deprivation started after day 2. We drop days 0-1, and make the
baseline to be new 0.

```{python}
#| label: load-data
sleepstudy = bmb.load_data("sleepstudy")
sleepstudy = sleepstudy[sleepstudy["Days"] >= 2].copy()
sleepstudy["Days"] = sleepstudy["Days"] - 2.
sleepstudy["Subject"] = sleepstudy["Subject"].astype("category")
sleepstudy.head()
```

Plot the data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-data
#| code-fold: true
subjects = sleepstudy["Subject"].unique()
n_subjects = len(subjects)
ncols = 6
nrows = int(np.ceil(n_subjects / ncols))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, sharex=True, sharey=True, figsize=(10, 6))
axes = axes.ravel()
for ax, subject in zip(axes, subjects):
    idx = sleepstudy["Subject"] == subject
    ax.plot(sleepstudy.loc[idx, "Days"], sleepstudy.loc[idx, "Reaction"], "o", alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title(f"Subject: {subject}", fontdict={"fontsize": 12})

for ax in axes[n_subjects:]:
    ax.axis("off")

fig.text(0.5, 0, "Days", ha="center")
fig.text(0, 0.5, "Reaction time (ms)", va="center", rotation="vertical");
```

we create a convenience function to plot the posterior conditional effects of the models.

```{python}
def plot_predictions(model, idata, model_name):
    _plot = bmb.interpret.plot_predictions(model, idata, "Days", use_hdi=False)

    plot = (
        _plot
        .add(so.Dot(color="k", marker="."), data=sleepstudy, x="Days", y="Reaction")
        .label(
            y="Reaction time (ms)", 
            title=model_name
        )
    )
    plot.show()
```

## Simple linear model

Prior base.

```{python}
prior_lin_base = {
    "Intercept": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=200, sigma=100),
    "Days": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=20),
    "sigma": bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02),
}
```

Model base and sample from the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: fit-lin-base
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
mod_lin_base = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior_lin_base,
)
idata_lin_base = mod_lin_base.fit(random_seed=SEED)
#mod_lin_base.compute_log_likelihood(idata_lin_base)
mod_lin_base.predict(idata_lin_base, kind="response", inplace=True, random_seed=SEED)
```

Posterior summary.

```{python}
az.summary(idata_lin_base, var_names="~mu", kind="stats")
```

Posterior conditional effects.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-conditional-effects-lin-base
plot_predictions(mod_lin_base, idata_lin_base, "Simple linear model")
```

## Simple linear model (centered predictors)

Points to discuss:

- priors on original or centered intercept?
- dependency of the prior on marginal moments of the data?
- different qualitative options for priors on b and sigma

Prior 1.

```{python}
prior1 = {
    "Intercept": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=250, sigma=100),
    "Days": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=20),
    "sigma": bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02),
}
```

Sample from prior 1 (prior predictive checking).

```{python}
#| label: fit1-prior
mod1_prior = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior1,
)
mod1_prior.build()
idata1_prior = mod1_prior.prior_predictive(draws=100, random_seed=SEED)
```

Prior predictive checking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-pp-check-fit1-prior
pc = az.plot_ppc_dist(idata1_prior, group="prior_predictive",
                      kind="ecdf",  

)
```

Model 1: sample from the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: fit1
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
mod1 = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior1,
)
idata1 = mod1.fit(random_seed=SEED)
mod1.predict(idata1, kind="response", random_seed=SEED)
```

Posterior summary.

```{python}
az.summary(idata1, var_names="~mu")
```

Posterior conditional effects.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-conditional-effects-fit1
plot_predictions(mod1, idata1, "Simple linear model")
```

Posterior predictive checking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-pp-check-fit1
pc = az.plot_ppc_dist(idata1)
```

Prior sensitivity analysis.

```{python}
mod1.compute_log_likelihood(idata1)
mod1.compute_log_prior(idata1)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-priorsense-fit1
az.plot_psense_dist(idata1, var_names="~mu",
                    visuals={"dist":False}
)
```

## Simple linear model (informative priors)

Points to discuss:

- Priors will be influencing the posterior if chosen to be informative enough
- For models that are simple relative to the amount of data, prior distributions
  are unlikely to affect the posterior strongly, unless prior are very informative

Prior 2.

```{python}
prior2 = {
    "Intercept": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=250, sigma=100),
    "Days": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=1),
    "sigma": bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02),
}
```

Model 2: sample from the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: fit2
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
mod2 = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior2,
)
idata2 = mod2.fit(random_seed=SEED)
mod2.predict(idata2, kind="response", random_seed=SEED)
```

Posterior summary.

```{python}
az.summary(idata2, var_names="~mu", kind="stats")
```

Posterior conditional effects.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-conditional-effects-fit2
plot_predictions(mod2, idata2, "Model 2")
```

Prior sensitivity analysis.

```{python}
mod2.compute_log_likelihood(idata2)
mod2.compute_log_prior(idata2)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-priorsense-fit2
az.plot_psense_dist(idata2, var_names="~mu",
                    visuals={"dist":False}
)
```

## Simple linear model (informative priors with fat tails)

Points to discuss:
- tails of the priors (normal vs. Student-t)

Prior 2b.

```{python}
prior2b = {
    "Intercept": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=250, sigma=100),
    "Days": bmb.Prior("StudentT", nu=7, mu=0, sigma=1),
    "sigma": bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02),
}
```

Model 2b: sample from the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: fit2b
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
mod2b = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior2b,
)
idata2b = mod2b.fit(random_seed=SEED)
mod2b.predict(idata2b, kind="response", random_seed=SEED)
```

Posterior summary.

```{python}
az.summary(idata2b, var_names="~mu")
```

Posterior conditional effects.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-conditional-effects-fit2b
plot_predictions(mod2b, idata2b, "Model 2b")
```

Prior sensitivity analysis.

```{python}
mod2b.compute_log_likelihood(idata2b)
mod2b.compute_log_prior(idata2b)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sleepstudy-priorsense-fit2b

)
```

Illustrate difference between normal and Student-t prior.

```{python}
#| label: fig-compare-normal-student-density
pz.Normal(0, 1).plot_pdf()
pz.StudentT(7, 0, 1).plot_pdf()
```

Compute CI-bound for an exponential prior.

```{python}
pz.Exponential(0.02).ppf([0.025, 0.975])
```

## Linear varying intercept model

Points to discuss:

- How to represent unidimensional multilevel structures via priors
- priors on hyperparameters (SDs)
- shall the prior on sigma change now that we add more terms?

Prior 3.

```{python}
prior3 = {
    "Intercept": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=250, sigma=100),
    "Days": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=20),
    "sigma": bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02),
    "1|Subject": bmb.Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=bmb.Prior("Exponential", lam=0.02)),
}
```

Model 3: sample from the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: fit3
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
mod3 = bmb.Model(
    "Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject)",
    sleepstudy,
    priors=prior3,
    categorical="Subject",
)
idata3 = mod3.fit(random_seed=SEED)
mod3.predict(idata3, kind="response", random_seed=SEED)
```

Posterior summary.

```{python}
az.summary(idata3, var_names=["~mu", "~1|Subject"])
```

Posterior conditional effects per subject.

```{python}
_plot = bmb.interpret.plot_predictions(mod3, idata3, ["Days", "Subject"], use_hdi=False,
    subplot_kwargs={"main": "Days", "panel": "Subject"},
    fig_kwargs={"theme": {"figure.figsize": (12, 7)}, 
                "title": "subject {}".format,
                "wrap": 6,
                })
plot = (
    _plot
    .add(
        so.Dot(color="k", marker=".", artist_kws={"zorder": 0}), 
        data=sleepstudy, 
        x="Days", 
        y="Reaction",
        col="Subject"
    )
)
plot.show()
```
